question: A communications manager needs a twelve-page annual review written. She wants to catch problems early rather than after a full draft exists. What should she ask for as the first stage?
options: A) A section-by-section outline naming what each section covers, which she can correct before any prose is written.
B) A list of every source document that the review will need, so that she can gather all of them before writing begins.
C) The opening two pages written in full, so she can judge the tone and standard the rest will be written to.
D) A full first draft written quickly, on the understanding that she will mark it up heavily on her first read.
correct_answers: A) A section-by-section outline naming what each section covers, which she can correct before any prose is written.
explanations: Correct. An outline is the cheapest artefact that still exposes the decisions that matter: coverage, emphasis and order. Correcting it takes minutes, whereas the same corrections applied to finished prose mean rewriting most of it.
A source list is a useful piece of preparation, but it says nothing about what the review will argue or how it will be organised.
Finished opening pages test tone but not structure, and the review's real risk is that the wrong things are covered in the wrong proportion.
Marking up a complete draft is precisely the expensive rework she is trying to avoid, since structural changes at that point mean rewriting whole sections.
